content: Warnings Anaphylaxis Severe and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in patients receiving penicillin therapy. These reactions are more likely to occur in individuals with a prior history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. Patients with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity have also experienced severe reactions when treated with cephalosporins. Before starting therapy with Bicillin L-A, it is essential to thoroughly investigate the patient’s history of hypersensitivity to penicillins, cephalosporins, or other allergens. If an allergic reaction occurs, Bicillin L-A must be discontinued immediately, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Severe anaphylactic reactions require urgent emergency management, including the administration of epinephrine. Clostridium difficile-Associated Diarrhea (CDAD) Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with the use of nearly all antibacterial agents, including Bicillin L-A. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. Antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile. This bacterium produces toxins A and B, which contribute to the development of CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may not respond to standard antimicrobial therapy and could require surgical intervention, such as colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea after antibiotic use. A thorough medical history is crucial, as CDAD has been reported to occur up to two months after the administration of antibiotics. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotics not directed against C. difficile may be necessary. Appropriate management, including fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation, should be initiated as clinically indicated. Precautions General Bicillin L-A should only be prescribed when there is a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a valid prophylactic indication. Using this medication inappropriately increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Penicillin should be used cautiously in patients with a history of significant allergies or asthma. Care must be taken to avoid intravenous or intra-arterial administration, as well as injection near major peripheral nerves or blood vessels, as these routes can cause neurovascular damage. Prolonged use of antibiotics may lead to the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, including fungi. Information for Patients Patients should be informed that diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and typically resolves after the antibiotic is discontinued. However, if watery or bloody stools occur, with or without abdominal cramps and fever, even up to two months after completing the antibiotic course, patients should contact their physician immediately. Patients should also be counseled that Bicillin L-A and other antibacterial drugs are only effective against bacterial infections and do not treat viral infections, such as the common cold. When prescribed Bicillin L-A, patients should be instructed to take the medication exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or failing to complete the full course of treatment may reduce the effectiveness of the therapy and increase the risk of developing antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Laboratory Tests In cases of streptococcal infections, treatment must be sufficient to eradicate the organism completely. Failure to do so may result in complications associated with streptococcal disease. Cultures should be obtained after completing therapy to confirm the elimination of streptococci. Drug Interactions The bacteriostatic antibiotic tetracycline may antagonize the bactericidal effects of penicillin. Therefore, concurrent use of these drugs should be avoided. Co-administration of penicillin and probenecid increases and prolongs serum penicillin levels by reducing its renal excretion. This occurs because probenecid competitively inhibits the renal tubular secretion of penicillin. Pregnancy Category B Reproductive studies in animals, including mice, rats, and rabbits, have not shown evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus due to penicillin G. Human data from the use of penicillins during pregnancy have not demonstrated adverse effects on the fetus. However, there are no well-controlled studies in pregnant women to conclusively rule out potential risks. As animal studies are not always predictive of human outcomes, penicillin G benzathine should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary. Nursing Mothers Soluble penicillin G is excreted in breast milk. Caution should be exercised when administering penicillin G benzathine to nursing mothers. Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility No long-term animal studies have been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic, mutagenic, or fertility-impairing potential of this drug. Pediatric Use Refer to the Indications and Usage and Dosage and Administration sections for specific guidance on pediatric use. Geriatric Use Clinical studies of penicillin G benzathine have not included sufficient numbers of patients aged 65 and older to determine whether their responses differ from those of younger patients. However, other clinical experience has not identified significant differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. In general, dosing for elderly patients should be cautious, starting at the lower end of the dosing range. This approach reflects the higher likelihood of decreased hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of other medical conditions or concurrent drug therapies in this population. Since penicillin G is substantially excreted by the kidneys, the risk of toxic reactions may be higher in patients with impaired renal function. Therefore, renal function should be monitored, and dose adjustments may be necessary in elderly patients.
